newsitem.title: NORWAY: Perry cautions NATO on scope of mission in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Perry cautions NATO on scope of mission in Bosnia.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry cautioned NATO defence ministers on Wednesday against giving police duties to any new military force in Bosnia and emphasised that his country was cool about sending troops to hunt down indicted war criminals, senior U.S. officials said.

The officials, who asked not to be identified, told reporters that the United States supported a move on Wednesday to begin planning for new peacekeepers to replace the current NATO-led peace implementation force (IFOR) next year, but had made no decision on whether to participate.

The United States at present has 15,000 troops in Bosnia as part of the 52,000-member IFOR and is gauging whether to take part in any new force next year. Key allies have said they would take part only if the United States did so.

A senior U.S. defence official said Perry made clear at the opening session of a two-day ministerial meeting in Bergen that, if the United States took part in a new force, it was not anxious to see troops to assume civil tasks such as breaking up fights or overseeing civilian police at every turn.
"We need to find a way to strengthen the international police effort" in Bosnia, the official said.
"I don't think anybody, not just the United States, is anxious...to send a future force to provide a general police function in the country," the official added.

The U.S. officials said that Perry was also cool to calls from some western officials such as German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe to broaden the current IFOR mandate in any new force and to actively hunt down indicted war criminals such as former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb army commander, General Ratko Mladic.
"I think everybody knows it is important to support the war crimes tribunal, (but) launching individual manhunts is a very different mission," said one official.
"I think it would not be one (mission) that the United States would be prepared to urge on the alliance. That has been our position all during the IFOR period and I don't think it would change."

Western sources at the meeting indicated privately that Germany, Canada, the Netherlands and Turkey had shown interest in expanding the mandate of any new force to include a possible active search for indicted war criminals.

Perry himself told reporters on arrival in Bergen on Tuesday that flat predictions by Ruehe and others that a new peacekeeping force would go to Bosnia after the IFOR mission ended in December were "premature".
His statement mirrored continuing caution on a new Bosnia force by the government of President Bill Clinton ahead of the November 5 U.S. presidential election.

But the U.S. defence official told reporters on Wednesday that the United States was "prepared to make the decision when it has to be made," based on an alliance timetable "which could be before (or) could be after the United States presidential election".

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov will attend a special Thursday session of the NATO meeting and he and Perry will have bilateral talks following the special meeting of the NATO and Russian defence chiefs.

Rodionov, Perry and Norway's defence minister, Joergen Kosmo, will also sign an agreement on Thursday under which the three nations will cooperate to clean up nuclear and other waste dumped or stored by Russia's military in the Arctic.
